dehydrated_text:
Jesus tells the story of how God has prepared a great feast for us, but the rich won’t go because they're too busy making money. Paul teaches us that it's the rich who will lead us to the kingdom because the rich can finance the spreading of Christianity. What matters is metrics that help us spread Christianity—how many souls are we saving by converting people? How cohesive is our church? That’s all care Paul cares about; he's a business person.

Okay, Jesus is a prophet, but Paul is a business person. And so it is Paul who really is the spiritual god of Christianity, not Jesus.

At this time in history—maybe around 40-50 AD—there are lots of different Christianities because Jesus taught that the kingdom of heaven is within you, making it very diverse and democratic. Early leaders like Mary Magdalene tend to be wealthy and charismatic. But by the time you hit Paul's Christianity, it’s anti-woman; there's a strict hierarchy and orthodoxy.

In other words, early Christians may have been persecuted, but they were being persecuted by Paul as much as by the Romans. At this time, the Catholic Church is only a very small minority because for most people, Jesus’ teachings are more appealing than Paul’s emphasis on obedience and sacrifice.

So, when Jesus dies in 30 AD, it's a very small group of people, but Christianity spreads quickly. This spread built the foundations for what becomes the Catholic Church by 300 AD, with Paul being crucial to its growth.

Jesus’ poetry spreads quickly throughout the empire because it’s easy to memorize. But once Paul builds the structure of Christianity based on Roman patterns, it spreads even quicker and eventually wins out until it conquers the entire Roman Empire. Scholars agree that Paul is the founder of Christianity, but three mysteries remain unsolved: why a literate and wealthy Jew like Paul joined a movement of illiterate Jewish peasants; why he converted from hunting Christians to becoming a fanatical follower of Jesus; and where did he get the money to support his travels and secretaries?

Clearly, some see him as a spy working for either the Roman Empire or Jewish leaders. The Bible says that the Jews killed Jesus, but this is confusing given the reasons we discussed in class—Jews don’t kill each other.

The key point is that Paul's strategic and business-like approach to spreading Christianity was critical to its rapid growth and eventual dominance.
